# 32 Well-Designed UX Portfolio Examples

Last Updated
January 7 2026


![Juhil Mendpara](<Base64-Image-Removed>)

Written By [Juhil Mendpara](https://www.sitebuilderreport.com/juhil-mendpara)

More so than any other professional’s website, a UX designer’s portfolio site should be perfect. After all, potential clients and employers expect a top-notch experience on your ⁠— a user experience designer’s ⁠— portfolio site.

Of course, as a UX designer, you intuitively know what a great website experience looks like:

- You know the best UX portfolio sites get out of the way and showcase the UX designer’s work;
- You know the site should be clean, accessible, and easy to use;
- You might also know the essential pages your UX portfolio website must include - an about section to tell your story, case studies, your design process, testimonials, and a contact form, among other things.

But there are a lot of ways to showcase all the details and design the website surrounding it. Get inspired by the following UX designer portfolio examples to make your ideal UX portfolio.

_Tip:_ Use ← and → arrow keys to browse.

## [1\. Aarron Walter](https://www.aarronwalter.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Aarron Walter , from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.aarronwalter.com/)

Aarron Walter is a creative team leader with vast experience. He was the fourth hire at Mailchimp, where he became the Director of UX. Then, he joined InVision as VP of Design Education, and most recently, he was the Director Of Product at Resolve to Save Lives. He is also the author of “Designing for Emotion.”

Aarron’s simple yet effective personal-cum-portfolio website shows his expertise by a) being a well-designed website and b) showcasing his work. Let’s take a closer look:

- His work is unmissable: The hero section talks about the “professional him.” and has links to portfolio pages on obvious anchor texts. Just below it is the ‘A brief history’ section, which, again, leads to the portfolio pages. The same goes for the ‘My work’ section below it. He also has the links to his resume, social media profiles, and email in the hero section.
- Each portfolio page shows his work, his roles, his processes, the work’s impact, and testimonials from peers. All the information follows an obvious visual hierarchy.
- You can learn more about him and contact him from the navigation bar or footer links.

## [2\. Shawn Weston](http://www.sweston.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Shawn Weston, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](http://www.sweston.com/)

Shawn is an expert in UX design, illustration, writing, and more. He has been creating awesome designs for over 15 years, including some for popular brands like Mastercard and GrubHub.

His website follows the latest minimalist web design practices well. For instance, he uses an easy-to-read font combination and a simple gray (background) and black (text) color palette. Moreover, the site homepage has just two elements:

1. The central paragraph introduces Shawn, his style, experience, and design thinking process.
2. The navigation links to crucial pages like his resume and UX portfolio.

The UX portfolio includes some big names and extended case studies of the work he has done for them. Each case study starts with a title and a concise description of the UX project. Then, he conveys everything he and his team did in detail and with relevant visuals.

**Note** : I skimmed through Shawn’s Grubhub UX project case study. It’s SO long that you’ll need about two hours to read it thoroughly. But everything’s to the point, so the length is justified. You shouldn’t make a long case study just for the sake of it; in fact, you should try to [shorten it as much as possible.](https://bootcamp.uxdesign.cc/how-to-fix-your-long-a-s-ux-case-studies-da9b54f72f40)

## [3\. Mike Wilson](https://iammikewilson.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Mike Wilson, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://iammikewilson.com/)

Mike Wilson is a designer working in the Seattle area. He is an expert in UX research, interaction design, and visual design. His love for figuring out how consumers can easily interact with a platform has landed him projects in many different fields.

I love how Mike has used his photo as the homepage background ⁠— it gives the website an immediate personal touch. Unfortunately, though, I am not a fan of using bare minimum text top of the fold ⁠— “I am Mike Wilson” is good, but some mention of his profession alongside would have been ideal.

Besides that tiny complaint, everything about Mike’s UX portfolio site is superb. Below the image, he does give a short introduction about who he is and what he does. He has also listed three UX case studies right below the ‘About me’ section.

Each UX project case study is well put. Mike mentions his role, who the client was, what the challenges were, what research & planning he or his teammates did, how he designed the solution, etc. He also includes sketches, early prototypes, wireframes, and other visual elements. He ends his case studies with a conclusion wherein he mentions what he’d do differently if he were to take on the same project again ⁠— _I love it!_

## [4\. Moritz Oesterlau](https://www.moritzoesterlau.de/)

[Made With \\
Webflow](https://webflow.grsm.io/sbr?sid1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Moritz Oesterlau, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.moritzoesterlau.de/)

Moritz teaches UX design as a tutor at CareerFoundry and also has web design, branding, and UX projects under his cap.

His portfolio website, as he proudly puts it, was reviewed and approved by the grand Ran Segall, the founder of Flux Academy. That’s proof enough that this UX portfolio is on point. Let me just highlight the elements I like:

- **Easy navigation & visual hierarchy**: Visitors would want to know about Moritz, see his work, and contact him if they like it. This portfolio gives all three front and center.
- **Formatting**: Moritz’s case studies are comprehensive, with in-depth descriptions of all the steps he went through for the project (from identifying challenges and making user personas to conclusions). Yet, they are easy to follow, thanks to the formatting. Some examples:
![Most UX portfolios take a lot more space to describe these.](https://ucarecdn.com/d4defe1c-f2f2-45d3-8aaa-f93701cc2df8/)![The cards, instead of plain text or bullet points, look nice.](https://ucarecdn.com/f6a4922f-7880-4ef6-9018-01c0aaa56da0/)

## [5\. Gloria Lo](https://www.glorialo.design/)

[Made With \\
Webflow](https://webflow.grsm.io/sbr?sid1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Gloria Lo, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.glorialo.design/)

Gloria Lo is in Sydney, Australia, working on UX/UI design for software products. She currently works at Canva as a senior product designer. She also sings, paints, and writes.

Her website is a showcase for both her work and play. The UX work portfolio is the primary, so it’s at the top of the visual hierarchy:

1. The minimal homepage lists her three recent projects in clean sections—the first of which is visible above the fold.
2. In the navigation bar, too, work comes before play.

Clicking on each portfolio item will take you to the corresponding case study.

Case studies are comprehensive yet never feel overwhelming. Sections are well-defined and in obvious positions. They have a screenshot of the final results at the top, then comes sections (from top to bottom): overview & Gloria’s role in the project, background info, the process & understanding the problem(s), insights, prioritization of issues, wireframing/designs, etc., ending with the results and takeaways.

![](https://ucarecdn.com/3aa0a48c-409f-4d95-a821-3b8796747f8e/)

The “Play” dropdown menu takes you to her music, art, and blog page. They are also well-designed. For example, the [art portfolio page resembles the best](https://www.sitebuilderreport.com/inspiration/art-portfolios):

![](https://ucarecdn.com/51bcb4f7-3283-4476-98ee-eaa3056a1818/)

## [6\. Jeff Shibasaki](https://jeffshibasaki.com/)

[Made With \\
Wordpress](https://www.wqwln8trk.com/2CW6XNM57/TZ3X1FRR/)

[![Screenshot of Jeff Shibasaki, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://jeffshibasaki.com/)

Jeff Shibasaki is a certified UX writer and content designer from Atlanta. Currently, he is the UX writer at Gympass. He is also an amateur UX designer.

For aspiring UX designers, Jeff’s UX portfolio could be a great inspiration. From what it seems, Jeff hasn’t done any professional UX design work. However, he has multiple UX redesign projects for brands like LinkedIn, Berkshire Hathaway, The New York Times, etc. How? Those are unsolicited work Jeff probably did on his own time to showcase his UX design skills.

Though none of the UX portfolio items are real, each case study is well put together with appropriate sections experienced professionals use in their UX portfolio.

## [7\. Kelly Batchelor](https://www.kellybatchelor.com/)

[Made With \\
Wordpress](https://www.wqwln8trk.com/2CW6XNM57/TZ3X1FRR/)

[![Screenshot of Kelly Batchelor, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.kellybatchelor.com/)

Kelly is based in the UK and is excited about each and every project she’s given. Kelly Batchelor loves creating and problem-solving using design skills that are always completed with energy and art.

You’ll see only two (important) things on her website when you open it:

1. A short intro: “Hey, I’m Kelly. I’m a Product Designer from London, UK.”
2. Navigation links to her ‘Work’ and ‘About’ page.

The ‘Work’ link doesn’t direct to a separate case studies page but opens a drop-down list of her case studies on hover. **I suggest you don’t use such drop-down lists** ⁠— instead, create a separate ‘case studies’ page which people can visit by clicking ‘Work’. That way, you can give proper context for each case study, and visitors can open whichever they find suitable.

For case studies, she follows the typical UX designer case study layout that starts with defining the problem and then goes on to processes and ends with a conclusion. However, there are two web design choices she makes that you might want to replicate in your UX portfolio:

**1\. Showing the final design screenshot alongside the project title/description**. This way, clients will know how her UX design work looks right away. In most case studies, the client has to scroll until the end to find the final product, which they might not do.

![](https://ucarecdn.com/2e0328f6-c818-4d10-b4c0-a846b6c8c849/)

**2\. Ending with a “More Projects” section**. Because of it, potential clients can read another case study if the particular case study they saw didn’t impress them.

![](https://ucarecdn.com/47d7eb6f-1385-4e5c-b161-775a7d82f9ef/)

## [8\. Pratibha Joshi](https://www.pratibhajoshi.com/)

[Made With \\
Wordpress](https://www.wqwln8trk.com/2CW6XNM57/TZ3X1FRR/)

[![Screenshot of Pratibha Joshi, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.pratibhajoshi.com/)

Pratibha is a product designer at Google and has previously worked for Microsoft and Sprinklr. She loves to create delightful human experiences, which is apparent from her UX portfolio.

Her website homepage is straightforward and, therefore, copy-worthy (if that’s even a word). At the top, she has her photo and a short description of her professional self. Then there’s a simple navigation bar with links to her ‘About me,’ ‘Contact,’ and ‘Experiments’ pages.

The work/case studies section is located on the homepage itself. I would’ve loved a jump link to the section in the navigation bar, but this is accessible in just one scroll, so it works.

Most of her UX portfolio is password-protected, but I did see her case study for _BJP Connect_ \- a single app for large group communication and work management. It’s perfect: She uses screenshots of the final product at the top, gives an overview of the project and her role in it, and then writes about the whole process with visuals (like videos of her interacting with each screen).

Overall, the UX professional’s website is typical. **There’s just one extra page** : _Experiments_. There she showcases the UX experiments she does in her free time. I think it’s fantastic: It shows her passion for what she does professionally.

## [9\. Lu Yu Portfolio](https://luyu.co/)

[Made With \\
Wordpress](https://www.wqwln8trk.com/2CW6XNM57/TZ3X1FRR/)

[![Screenshot of Lu Yu Portfolio, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://luyu.co/)

Lu Yu does interaction design & art direction. She was Head Of Brand at Pitch and is a Jury member of Awwwards & Digital Design award.

The fact that she is a jury member of a top professional web design and development competition body would assumably make it a given that her website will be on point. Is it? Well, let me try to evaluate it using Awwwards’ evaluation system criteria (Side Note: I don’t think I am eligible to be an Awwwards jury).

Awwwards ranks based on the following 4 criteria:

- Design: 40% points
- Usability: 30% points
- Creativity: 20% points
- Content: 10% points

**Design**-wise, Lu Yu’s website is awesome:

- It has great, consistent colors.
- Transitions, microinteractions, and animations are fantastic.
- Typography is distinctive and legible.
- Negative space is used well.
- Screenshots and other images are high quality.

None of the aesthetic elements interfere with **usability**.

- The website is mobile responsive and loads pretty fast.
- Contact details and links to her Dribbble and Behance profiles are at the top.
- Since the portfolio items and ‘about’ section come soon enough in the visual hierarchy of the homepage, there’s no need for links to them in the navigation bar—so it’s sorted.
- Portfolio items are presented neatly, and it’s clear that clicking on them opens a separate case study page (thanks to the on-hover animation).
- The content organization is also pretty standard, which is good.

On the scale of not-creative-at-all to outlandishly **creative**, this portfolio website has the right balance. It definitely has its own character, but the creativity never harms the usability like many super-creative sites do (many of which you can find on Awwwards itself).

I think this UX portfolio can do better with **content**.

- First off, the hero text, “A COLLECTION OF ARTIFACTS Made with love & purpose.” fails to communicate that it is a UX designer’s portfolio site — it doesn’t matter much as her potential clients will likely have the proper context, but clear communication is always better.
- Second, the project/case study pages have a lot of screenshots of her work, which is good (as they say: show, don’t tell), but there’s pretty much no text at all, which makes the page look cramped. Plus, case study pages on other UX portfolio sites are better because they describe problems, design processes they used, etc.

**Overall, Lu Yu’s site is superbly designed and made keeping usability/user experience in mind.**

## [10\. Niya Watkins](https://www.niyawatkins.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Niya Watkins, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.niyawatkins.com/)

Niya is a UI/UX Designer with a passion for creating user experiences that make life easier. She is from Washington, DC, and currently works on reader experience for _The Atlantic_.

Her website is simple in a good way. The home page has no images, just text that introduces her and her best work. Most of her case studies are password-protected, but you can read her work on Spotify Social Feature.

Then there’s the hamburger menu that helps you navigate to other important pages like ‘About’ and ‘Contact’.

Overall, Niya’s UX portfolio is solid. But if there’s one thing you’d want to imitate from Niya’s site, it’d be the storytelling style she uses in the about section. Here’s how she describes transitioning from working in International Affairs to becoming a freelance UX designer:

![](https://ucarecdn.com/d7807ad5-fcf2-440a-ac92-533c76dbdcd3/)

## [11\. Sophie Brittain](https://www.sophiebritt.com/)

[Made With \\
Wix](https://wix.pxf.io/c/41544/2097939/25616?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Sophie Brittain, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.sophiebritt.com/)

Sophie was born and raised in Houston. She now works as a product designer in New York and has worked on design projects for brands like Kia and Cadillac Fairview.

Her website is to the point. Above the fold, you’ll see a short intro of Sophie and navigation links to her ‘Work’ and ‘About’ sections. You’ll find links to contact her and her social media profiles in the footer. In my opinion, adding a CTA like “Contact me” at the top is better because sometimes potential clients are already impressed by you (say from your social media posts), and they just want to get in touch.

All her case studies are password-protected, so I can’t comment much on them or the website design surrounding them. However, I can see the thumbnails, and it seems she does a fantastic UX designing job.

One thing I don’t quite like (or don’t appreciate) is this animation she uses besides her logo/site title. Seems more distracting than useful to me.

![](https://ucarecdn.com/b87f8387-ed71-4085-8681-cc4eb4674426/)

## [12\. Amy Wu](http://www.amywutoo.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Amy Wu, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](http://www.amywutoo.com/)

Amy is a product designer at Microsoft. She delivers people-first designs and currently leads user research for _Money in Excel_, a Microsoft 365 solution subscribers can use to manage, track, and analyze money and spending, all in Excel.

Her UX portfolio website’s homepage is an excellent example of showcasing the most essential things top of the fold. She introduces herself and sums up her extensive career right at the top in beautiful yet clear typography. She has also added a confident picture of her interacting with her team below the intro. Overall, potential clients will know pretty much everything about the “professional Amy” as soon as they land on her website.

The next element in the website’s visual hierarchy is her top navigation bar. It includes links to the important pages (for her): About, Work, and Writing. If your aim with the website is to get clients (that’s probably not Amy’s website goal) and you’d be mimicking Amy’s website, perhaps replacing “Writing” with “Contact” or a similar CTA will be a better idea.

**Just like the homepage, she showcases her case studies perfectly too.** Each case study is in-depth with relevant information about the UX project. They include background, timeline, goal, success metric, problem, research, deliverables, prototyping and usability testing, and more. She also uses screenshots and videos to show her work effectively.

## [13\. Olga Rody](https://olgarody-portfolio-site.webflow.io/)

[Made With \\
Webflow](https://webflow.grsm.io/sbr?sid1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Olga Rody, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://olgarody-portfolio-site.webflow.io/)

Just enter this site, and you’ll know it is of Olga Rody, a UI/UX designer based in Indiana, US (thanks to the giant fonts).

The heart in the logo and the hero section communicates Olga’s love for UX. The passion for UX, though, wasn’t from the start of her career, as you’d discover if you open the ‘About’ page from the clearly labeled & visible navigation link: She started as an accountant in Ukraine and only discovered her passion for web design and later UX design when she moved to the US.

Scroll down a bit on the homepage, and you’ll learn she has worked for Easy Way, Bike Generation, Buddy, and YuTu Social. You can also click on the corresponding block to see case studies of her work with these companies.

On the case study pages, she clearly describes her roles, main goals, and her involvement in the work at the start. Then, the usual is showcased, including sections for discovery and user research, user persona, user flow, journey map, wireframes, usability testing, etc.

I also like her hand-drawn sketches—they give insight into her thinking process and understanding of design:

![](https://ucarecdn.com/4b8a7984-88a0-448c-a37c-d271e21257fc/)

## [14\. Elma Lin](https://www.elmalin.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Elma Lin , from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.elmalin.com/)

Elma is a UI/UX designer with 15+ years of experience with a background in graphic design and human-computer interaction.

She has designed her portfolio website efficiently. At the top, she introduces herself and shows a couple of her main projects with an option to see more. Directly below it is the footer, where she tells a bit more about herself, has links to download her resume, and mentions the design tools she is proficient in (Figma, InVision, UXPin, Adobe XD, etc.).

## [15\. Mizko](https://www.mizko.net/)

[Made With \\
Webflow](https://webflow.grsm.io/sbr?sid1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Mizko, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.mizko.net/)

Michael is a UX/UI designer who also teaches others to design through courses. He has worked with leading tech companies, including Google, Facebook, Apple, and Microsoft. He also creates excellent [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/mizko) content for aspiring UI/UX designers.

The Mizko website is superbly structured (and designed) for a site that promotes both a UX design studio and an education platform.

- The navigation has links to “Courses” and “Services”, i.e., both his offering. Plus, there’s a link to the “Testimonials” page (which acts as social proof for his course) and a link to the “Case studies” page (which is social proof for his services).
- He uses multiple CTAs top of the fold. Also, he creates urgency with the “Only 1 project spot left” text beside the “Contact” button.
- As you scroll on the website homepage, you’ll see another social proof in the form of the “Featured in” section, where he shows his work is featured in big publications like Y Combinator, TechCrunch, and Webflow.

Though Michael has a UX case studies page, he doesn’t have any case studies written. So he just shows them as “Coming soon”:

![](https://www.sitebuilderreport.com/inspiration/RackMultipart20220704-1-493y5n_html_cb51cfac88807791.png)

**This is a better way to go about it than not showing any proof of work at all**. If you are a freelancer or a small business, you might not have time to write case studies because an in-depth case study can take days or even a week to write. Therefore, just write the project title and description and label the case study as “coming soon”.

## [16\. Jessica Hernandez](https://www.jessicahernandez.me/)

[Made With \\
Webflow](https://webflow.grsm.io/sbr?sid1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Jessica Hernandez, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.jessicahernandez.me/)

Jessica is a UX researcher based in San Francisco, California.

Her website dazzles with its unique typography, colorful elements, and different microinteractions and animations. Yet, it succeeds at achieving the website goal, i.e., introducing her, showcasing her resume and user research projects, and giving potential clients her contact information. However…

I am not a fan of this playful use of 7-8 fonts on a single page. Almost all UX professionals will tell you not to use more than two or three fonts.

![This looks unprofessional and unstructured.](https://ucarecdn.com/3853589c-af3a-4c29-b25f-75eefba2bd2a/)

## [17\. Myriem Ech](https://myriemech.com/)

[Made With \\
Wordpress](https://www.wqwln8trk.com/2CW6XNM57/TZ3X1FRR/)

[![Screenshot of Myriem Ech, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://myriemech.com/)

Okay. So. There are a few things I REALLY like about this portfolio site. And others are just FRUSTRATING. If I were judging Myriem’s skills purely based on analyzing her site, I’d say she knows how to design a great UI but fails at giving a great experience.

### The Good:

Talk about putting work front and center, and Myriem’s UX/UI design portfolio nails it. Her work is presented in a neat two-column layout on the homepage. Plus, not only can you see all portfolio items, but each also has a slider of images that give an overview of her work’s results.

Moreover, she categorizes her projects to let visitors filter through: You can choose from three options — website, mobile app, and ecommerce — to see relevant works.

The top navigation is also clean - on the right is her name and designation; on the left is a noticeable CTA, links to her social media, and links to her About page and Blog page.

### The Bad:

Let’s start from the top.

1. You’d think clicking on her name/photo/logo will take you to the homepage. Wrong. It doesn’t do anything.
2. You’d think clicking on “See all projects” would do something, like probably take you to a separate portfolio page. Wrong. It’s just a jump link to the _projects_ section below it, so it does nothing.
3. You’d think that clicking on all the category icons (website, mobile app, ecommerce) will show you related projects. Kind of true. It does, but there are no ‘Mobile App’ projects, so clicking it does nothing.
4. You’d think clicking on any of the projects would take you to a separate case study page or something that’ll tell more about the project than a few screenshots and a vague title. Wrong. They are not clickable.

On top of it all, I found the loading time of this site on the higher side.

## [18\. Product Designer, Sun](https://www.sunyoungchouxui.com/)

[Made With \\
Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Product Designer, Sun, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.sunyoungchouxui.com/)

Sun designs products and experiences for brands in Commerce, Payments, and Retail. She currently works with Square.

Her website is very straightforward but loses some key elements:

- **The good**: As soon as you enter, you’ll see a well-written title, “From Concept to Product,” and a short bio. Next, you see thumbnails of the work she has done in a two-column gallery. She also has a page called “1-min idea” ⁠— here, she shows her new product design ideas, which reflects her passion for UX and design.
- **The bad**: You’ll have to hover over the thumbnails to get some idea about the case study/product/UX work she has done. Also, Sun doesn’t have an about page or anything that tells her story or shows who she is.

## [19\. Gautham Mukesh](https://www.gauthammukesh.com/)

[Made With \\
Wix](https://wix.pxf.io/c/41544/2097939/25616?subId1=inspiration/ux_portfolios)

[![Screenshot of Gautham Mukesh, from the ux portfolios collection.](<Base64-Image-Removed>)](https://www.gauthammukesh.com/)

Gautham Mukesh is a full-stack designer with experience in branding, development, illustration, web design, visual design, and UI/UX.

I love the landing page of this site. It has a fantastic scrolling animation that makes learning about Gautam, his projects, his processes, and contact information fun. However, I don’t like the fact that some elements that seem obviously clickable aren’t.

The case studies are also nicely written and designed. He shows the end result at the top and proceeds to describe the process of reaching there throughout the case study, which typically starts from objectives and challenges and ends with impact. One thing I’d have loved to see but isn’t on his case study pages: A link/button to see the next or previous case study at the end of each case study.

## [20\. Josie Allison](https://www.itsjosie.com/)

[Made With \\

With all the whitespace, this UX designer’s portfolio looks beautiful. Plus, it has well-presented, simple case studies.

## Frequently Asked Questions

#### Where can I build a UX portfolio?

You can build a personal UX portfolio site with an easy-to-use website builder like [Squarespace](https://squarespace.syuh.net/ZdXqDq) or an advanced platform like Webflow or WordPress. All have good templates for portfolio sites, but we recommend Squarespace because it'll be easiest of all to make a great UX portfolio site.

Alternatively, you can use a niche-specific platform like Cargo, Behance, UXfolio, etc.

#### What should a UX portfolio include?

The best UX portfolios include in-depth case studies, an about section, and a contact page. Besides, they have testimonials and 'featured in'' sections for social proof.

#### Do UX designers need a portfolio?

Absolutely! Most recruiters look at portfolios and case studies before hiring for any UX role.

#### How do I make a UX portfolio with no experience?

Do unsolicited work and showcase it as case studies like Jeff Shibasaki does.

# 79+ design statistics: Tools, collaboration, and AI in 2026

## Share 79+ design statistics: Tools, collaboration, and AI in 2026

## Explore more from

[Design basics](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-basics/)

## From wireframe to website, faster

Design, prototype, and refine every page.

[Get started for free](https://www.figma.com/signup)

![](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/5b68a71b5c8da981265853b797ad80f7afd96f78-1440x720.png?w=1440&h=720&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

Design decisions can be hard to explain, especially when the people you’re presenting to don’t speak the same visual language. While most teams agree that [good design](https://www.figma.com/blog/what-is-good-design-in-the-age-of-ai/) matters, stakeholders often want proof that it drives results.

That’s where data comes in. These design statistics help translate creative intuition into measurable impact, whether you’re justifying a choice, scoping a project, or building a case for investment.

Read on to learn:

- Current benchmarks for design salaries and remote work trends
- How AI is reshaping the creative landscape and designer skill sets
- Insights into team collaboration and process efficiency
- Key data on mobile responsiveness, page load expectations, and accessibility
- How design directly influences brand trust and ROI

## [**Design employment statistics**](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-statistics/\#design-employment-statistics)

Recent data paints a picture of a design workforce that’s adaptable, resilient, and increasingly happier with how they work. These design statistics are a snapshot of how designers are feeling about their careers, their workspaces, and the future of the profession.

01. 41% of [designers and developers](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/web-design-and-development/) say they were more satisfied with their job in 2024 than in 2023. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
02. Remote work is now the norm, with 97% of professionals working away from the office at least part time, and over half doing so fully. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
03. In Europe, 71% of designers and 75% of developers say they’re happy with their current workplace setup. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
04. Across the Asia-Pacific region, 70% of designers report being satisfied with their working arrangements. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
05. In the U.S., 62% of designers and 77% of developers express happiness with how and where they work. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
06. 45% of designers believe the job market has declined in recent years. [(Figma, 2025)](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/)
07. The global value of the [graphic design](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/what-is-graphic-design/) market is projected to pass $56 billion by the end of 2025. ( [NMSC, 2025](https://www.nextmsc.com/report/graphic-design-market))
08. Employment in graphic design is expected to remain stable, with a projected 2% growth rate through 2034. ( [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/graphic-designers.htm#:~:text=Median%20annual%20wages%2C%20May%202024,the%20average%20for%20all%20occupations))
09. The median annual pay for graphic designers in 2024 was $61,300, or $29.47 per hour. ( [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/graphic-designers.htm#:~:text=Median%20annual%20wages%2C%20May%202024,the%20average%20for%20all%20occupations))
10. The industry is pretty evenly split by sex: 50.2% of graphic designers in the U.S. are women, and 49.8% are men. ( [Zippia, 2025](https://www.zippia.com/graphic-designer-jobs/demographics/))
11. The average age of graphic designers in the U.S. is 38 years old. ( [Zippia, 2025](https://www.zippia.com/graphic-designer-jobs/demographics/))
12. 68% of graphic designers in the U.S. hold a bachelor’s degree. ( [Zippia, 2025](https://www.zippia.com/graphic-designer-jobs/demographics/))
13. 92% of business leaders expect employees in non-design roles to possess basic design skills and knowledge. ( [Canva, 2024](https://www.canva.com/visual-communications-report/2024/))

![According to Figma, 41% of designers and developers say they’re more satisfied with their job this year in 2025 than in 2024.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/503f5f6406b227bf3ac930cf02e4c1681473c86f-1440x800.png?w=1440&h=800&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

## [**AI in design statistics**](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-statistics/\#ai-in-design-statistics)

Artificial intelligence (AI) has quickly integrated into the design workflow of teams everywhere. While questions around trust and quality remain, the data shows that designers are embracing these tools to automate repetitive tasks and accelerate exploration. Here’s a look at how AI is currently reshaping the design process.

01. Looking ahead, 85% of designers and developers say AI will be essential to their future success. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
02. Efficiency is the main driver, with 78% of professionals saying that AI tools significantly speed up their workflows. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
03. However, only 58% say it improves the quality of their work. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
04. In the discovery phase, 38% of designers and 43% of developers use AI for customer research. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
05. 40% of designers and 29% of developers use AI for data analysis. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
06. In the design phase, 33% of designers use AI to generate design assets, 22% use it to create first drafts of interfaces or websites, and 21% use it to explore different layouts or themes. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
07. 40% of designers and developers don’t yet trust AI-generated outputs enough to rely on them fully. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
08. Strategic impact is still in question, as only 27% believe AI will significantly move the needle on company goals in the next year. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/ai-2025/))
09. More than half (56%) say AI makes them feel more hopeful about where design is headed. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
10. 86% of global creators report that they now use generative AI in their work. ( [Adobe, 2025](https://news.adobe.com/news/2025/10/adobe-max-2025-creators-survey))
11. 81% of creators say AI helps them produce content formats or styles they could not have created on their own. ( [Adobe, 2025](https://news.adobe.com/news/2025/10/adobe-max-2025-creators-survey))
12. 70% of creators express excitement about the potential of using AI agents that can execute tasks autonomously. ( [Adobe, 2025](https://news.adobe.com/news/2025/10/adobe-max-2025-creators-survey))
13. 85% of marketers and creatives report saving roughly four hours per week thanks to GenAI tools. ( [Canva, 2025](https://www.canva.com/marketing-ai-report/))
14. 77% of marketing and creative leaders agree that GenAI tools actively enhance their team's creative output. ( [Canva, 2025](https://www.canva.com/marketing-ai-report/))
15. 63% of professionals believe experimenting with AI has improved their ability to communicate visually, regardless of their job title. ( [Canva, 2025](https://www.canva.com/visual-communications-report/))
16. In just 10 years, the generative [AI design](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/ai-in-design/) sector is forecast to grow 18x its current size, from $741 million to $13.9 billion. ( [Precedence Research, 2024](https://www.precedenceresearch.com/generative-ai-in-design-market))
17. 35% of creative agencies say they use AI for design and branding purposes. ( [Function Point, 2025](https://functionpoint.com/resource/2025-creative-agency-trends-report))

![78% of designers and developers say AI tools speed up their workflows, but only 58% say it improves the quality of their work.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/74f5ef0cce3dbeec5c7ee00fac4ce19982eb9271-1440x800.png?w=1440&h=800&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

## [**Design workflow statistics**](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-statistics/\#design-workflow-statistics)

Great design requires constant collaboration between designers, developers, and stakeholders. [Collaborative tools](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/best-design-collaboration-tools/) have improved the process, but teams still face hurdles ranging from administrative busywork to the complex handoff between design and code. Here’s a look at how modern teams work together.

01. 84% of designers say they collaborate with developers at least weekly. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
02. 77% of designers with high work satisfaction use collaborative tools more often than those with lower satisfaction. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
03. 58% of satisfied designers use whiteboard tools more often than those with lower satisfaction. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
04. 91% of developers and 92% of designers believe the handoff process could be improved. ( [Figma, 2025](https://www.figma.com/reports/designer-developer-trends/))
05. 57% of creative teams spend more than a quarter of their total work time on non-creative tasks like file management and compliance. ( [Monotype, 2025](https://www.monotype.com/scaling-creative-operations))
06. Font version control is a major friction point, with 42% of creative professionals citing it as a specific challenge in their daily workflows. ( [Monotype, 2025](https://www.monotype.com/scaling-creative-operations))
07. Licensing complexity is also a challenge, with 68% of organizations facing hidden compliance risks related to their font usage. ( [Monotype, 2025](https://www.monotype.com/scaling-creative-operations))
08. 31% of creative agencies cite scope changes as their single biggest barrier to productivity this year. ( [Function Point, 2025](https://functionpoint.com/resource/2025-creative-agency-trends-report))
09. ‍91% of designers think designers and developers are at least sometimes “too different” to work together well. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
10. 81% of designers feel developers value their work. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
11. 57% of designers think developers are very open to feedback from designers. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
12. 39% of designers say the best way to improve collaboration is for designers and developers to learn each other’s skills. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
13. 28% believe that involving developers earlier in the design process would be the best solution, while 20% think that scheduling more meetings is the answer. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
14. Only 13% believe that bridging the gap between tools would help. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))
15. 40% believe that better collaboration would lead to higher-quality products. ( [CollabSoft, 2025](https://www.collabsoft.com/blog/designer-survey-2025))

![84% of designers say they collaborate with developers at least weekly.](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/599r6htc/regionalized/ca664a56d1dcfcff89f06269036f3ac163d1edd4-1440x750.png?w=1440&h=750&q=75&fit=max&auto=format)

## [**Web design statistics**](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/design-statistics/\#web-design-statistics)

Web design has evolved from strictly visual aesthetics to creating accessible experiences. As user expectations rise, the gap between a functioning site and a high-performing one often comes down to the details. The following statistics explore the current standards for [accessibility](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/creating-accessible-and-inclusive-design/), speed, and design complexity.

01. As of November 2025, there are 1.37 billion websites online, though only a fraction of these are actively maintained. ( [Netcraft, 2025](https://www.netcraft.com/blog/november-2025-web-server-survey))
02. 95% of companies agree that a professionally [designed UX](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/what-is-ux-design/) is critical to the success of startup mobile apps. ( [Goodfirms, 2025](https://www.goodfirms.co/resources/startup-mobile-app-ux-design-goodfirms-survey))
03. 80.3% of businesses rate usability as the single most important Web design factor, ranking it above visual aesthetics. ( [Goodfirms, 2025](https://www.goodfirms.co/resources/startup-mobile-app-ux-design-goodfirms-survey))
04. 90% of the lowest-performing e-commerce websites contain significant UX issues, compared to only 10% of top performers. ( [Reboot Online, 2025](https://www.rebootonline.com/seo-statistics/ecommerce-seo-statistics/))
05. User frustration is rampant, with 39.6% of all digital sessions now containing “frustration signals,” like rage clicks or dead clicks, due to poor interface design. ( [Contentsquare, 2024](https://contentsquare.com/digital-experience-benchmark/))
06. 94.8% of the world's top 1 million home pages still fail to meet basic WCAG 2 accessibility standards. ( [WebAIM, 2025](https://webaim.org/projects/million/))
07. 79.1% of home pages contain low-contrast text, making it the most common design failure on the Web today. ( [WebAIM, 2025](https://webaim.org/projects/million/))
08. The average home page displays 58.6 images. ( [WebAIM, 2025](https://webaim.org/projects/million/))

# Developer Portfolio Templates: Creating a Job-Winning Portfolio

As we enter into 2026 we've seen a huge change in the way that developers create their portfolio websites. The templates available now have much more than just a list of projects—they also include interactive elements, live code demonstrations, GitHub integration, and responsive design that draws the attention of both technical recruiters and hiring managers.

[By\\
\\
![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/UYoGYCvsbC5wHuO9Q76EX66OVCc.jpg?width=80&height=80)\\
\\
Anatolii Dmitrienko](https://x.com/bynneh)

\|

Mar 4, 2026

\|

10 Mins Read

![A smiling female developer works on a laptop in a modern high-rise office at sunset. Behind her, a large curved monitor displays a dark-mode portfolio website template featuring project cards, skills charts, a GitHub contribution graph, and navigation links.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/JgKD9FtkTXUA7k8pIh3cvyG4Qzw.jpg?width=1200&height=630)

The developer portfolio template that fits your needs best will help you effectively communicate your skills and value to potential employers or clients, whether you are a front-end developer designing beautiful user interfaces, a back-end developer building robust systems, or a full-stack developer doing both.

In this ultimate guide to developer portfolio templates, we will walk you through everything you want and need to know about developer portfolio templates, including the essential features that all developer portfolios should have and current design trends, as well as what platforms and customization strategies to help you stand out in today's competitive tech job market.

## What Are Developer Portfolio Templates?

Developer portfolio templates are pre-designed website templates specifically designed to be used by software developers, programmers and engineers to showcase technical skills, coding projects and professional experience. Unlike generic website templates, developer portfolio templates are very specific to the needs of developers—they provide capabilities such as displaying code snippets with syntax highlighting, integrating with version control platforms such as GitHub, showcasing live project demonstrations and providing accessible formats for technical documentation.

Today’s modern developer portfolio template includes many features intended to highlight the developer’s skills and knowledge of various technologies. Examples of these features are project showcase sections, skills visualisation sections, work experience timeline sections, education background sections, blog sections for demonstrating technical knowledge, and contact sections.

[![A minimalist developer portfolio website layout using the Praxis Framer template, featuring a clean project grid and dark mode interface.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/Kut2hrqGcwM2886i1U0pWcWc.jpg)](https://templifica.com/framer-templates/praxis)

A clean starting point often works best for technical portfolios.

[**Praxis**](https://templifica.com/framer-templates/praxis) is a free Framer template that removes unnecessary visual clutter. It focuses on the project gallery and technical skills. This approach is helpful for developers who want to launch a site within a few hours. It ensures the focus remains on the code and the problem-solving process, which is what hiring managers actually look for. Or, at least, it keeps things organized.

## High-quality developer portfolio templates include some essential features. These include:

1. Responsive and Mobile-First Design: Many recruiters and hiring managers use multiple devices to view portfolios. The responsive design of a template enables you to create a professional, eye-catching portfolio on all screen sizes (desktop, tablet, and smartphone). In addition, a mobile-first design will enhance your portfolio’s search ranking and offer a better user experience.

2. GitHub/Version Control Integration: A high-quality developer template allows integration with any version control system (GitHub, GitLab, BitBucket, etc.) to let you showcase your repository and contribution graphs directly on your portfolio. By doing this, developers provide recruiters with tangible evidence of their practice of coding, collaborating, and contributing to open-source. Technical recruiters view these traits as very valuable.

3. Project Showcase with Live Demos: Exceptional developer portfolios showcase their projects by offering their audience live demonstrations, published links, and detailed project case studies. The best templates provide project cards with a letter-box style image, badges showcasing the technology stack used, a short project description, and a written link to the site where the project is located and the source code repository.

4. Syntax Highlighted Code Snippets: Properly highlighting your code snippets demonstrates your attention to detail, the way you write code, and your coding style. A developer portfolio template supporting the syntax highlighting of the most used programming languages must support the easy-to-read and easy-to-understand formatting of code blocks.

5. Skills Visualisation/Technology Stack: The modern-day templates provide creative methods to display the technical skills of the developer, including horizontal skill progress bars, skill clouds, or the use of logo images that represent the technology stacks used. All of these visuals assist recruiters in quickly understanding the level of proficiency the developer has with technical languages, frameworks, and tools.

6. Performance Optimisation: Developers should create their portfolios based on best industry practices, which include the fast loading of their portfolios and the ability to optimise the performance of their portfolio templates. Using next generation technologies such as Next.js, React, or static site generators, the template should be able to load on all computers at lightning-fast speeds.

7. SEO Architecture: If a recruitment company searches for a developer with your particular skills, having a portfolio set up with proper SEO will increase the possibility that your portfolio shows up in search results. Quality templates should include semantic HTML, structured data, optimized images, and meta tags.


[![A professional multi-page Framer portfolio template for developers, showing structured case study sections and a clean, organized layout.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/2tivP5S4E3OddwKxNQUd28wsRuI.jpg)](https://templifica.com/framer-templates/fabrica)

Complex systems require a structured presentation.

[**Fabrica**](https://templifica.com/framer-templates/fabrica) template offers a comprehensive layout for multi-page portfolios. It includes specific sections for tech stacks, client testimonials, and long-form case studies which help in demonstrating professional growth over time. This framework is useful for senior developers with diverse project histories. Or rather, it provides the necessary space for deep technical explanations.

## 2026 Trends for Developer Portfolios

### 1\. Minimalist/Content-Focused Design

Developer portfolios will likely remain simple, clean, and minimalistic. The emphasis will remain on the developer's portfolio, which should have as few decorative features as possible. In contrast, Minimalist Design offers plenty of white space, clarity of information through typography and limited amounts of content will help your work to stand out.

### 2\. Interaction/3D Elements and Animation

By adding interactive elements to your portfolio and incorporating subtle animation, you can not only showcase your technical skills, you can also provide your visitors with an enjoyable experience. Combinations of 3D graphics; parallax scrolling; and hover effects will help to create depth within your portfolio without overwhelming the viewer.

### 3\. Dark Mode

Because most developers prefer a dark theme for their portfolios, many new portfolio templates will offer built-in dark mode functionality. Not only will this feature appeal to your target audience, it will also show that you are aware of your audience's preferences and the current web standards.

### 4\. Bold Typography/Creative Navigation

Using large, bold typography will create a strong visual impact. You can showcase your creativity with the typefaces you choose and provide creative navigation methods.

### 5\. Real-Time Data Integration

Many modern portfolios will connect real-time data directly from GitHub or Stack Overflow and provide you with a representation of your current coding activity; reputation score; problem-solving statistics and will demonstrate that you are active within the development community.

## Types of Developer Portfolio Templates

### Front-End Developer Templates

The front-end developer templates will showcase the visual aspect of your portfolio along with your UI/UX capabilities. Responsive design and CSS animation; as well as JavaScript interactions will demonstrate your proficiency in developing client-side applications.

### Developer Portfolios w/ Template TypesBack-End Developer Templates

Focus on API documentation, system architecture and design, database design and implementation tech. Include technical documentation, performance metrics and system diagrams as part of a back-end portfolio.

### FullStack Developer Templates

Integrate the front-end and back-end developer templates together to highlight skills in a variety of areas. An all-inclusive end-to-end development portfolio showing how each project was developed.

### Audience or Specialized Templates For Developers

Templates tailored for a particular niche market like Mobile or Game Developer, DevOps Engineer or Data Scientist are designed for the relative market for that niche.

## Homepage Containing A Clear Value Proposition

Your homepage should give visitors an immediate understanding of who you are, what you do and how you can provide additional value to them. Create an attractive and memorable homepage. An eye-catching headline, a professional picture, and a short introduction about yourself can create an impression.

### Featured Projects

View Your Featured ProjectsIn this section, include 3-6 of your best projects. Describe each project in detail including technology stacks, challenges encountered, and solutions implemented, and provide links to both live demo versions and source code repositories for each project.

### About Page with Your Story

Share how you got into programming, what interests you about programming, your work style, and what is motivating you as a programmer are things that help humanize the technical skills you have developed over time, and they enable employers to evaluate if you fit into their organisation's culture, as well as whether you are the right applicant for the role.

### Your Skills and Technologies

Provide a list of your technical skills categorised by category (Languages, Frameworks, Tools, and Methodologies) and an honest self-assessment of your level of proficiency for each skill.

### Your Work Experience and Education

A chronological record of your work and education. Provide the dates you worked in each organisation and your educational qualifications. Include the achievements and responsibilities that were part of your role.

### Your Blog or Articles

Publish articles on your technical knowledge and demonstrate your ability to communicate effectively as a member of the programming community. Publish your articles on your website to show you have thought leadership in this space.

### Your Contact Information and Calls to Action

Provide a number of contact options, allow recruiters to download your resume, and provide links to your social media accounts such as LinkedIn, GitHub, and Twitter.

### Customising Your Developer Portfolio Template

Change the layout, colours, and typography of your portfolio template to fit your personal branding while still maintaining a professional appearance. Use a colour scheme that complements the screenshots of your featured projects.

### Use Real Projects

Replace each placeholder project with an actual project that you have built. For each project, supply context, describe the contributions you made, the tools you used to build the project, and provide measurable results or lessons learned.

### Optimize Your Content for Your Target Audience

Adjust the content of your portfolio to match the specific roles or organizations that you are applying to. Highlight the projects you have completed that best demonstrate your technical abilities and the skills which align with the job descriptions of the positions you want.

### Analytics Implementation

Implement Google Analytics or similar tools to allow you to monitor visitor behaviour, popular projects, and visitor traffic sources. This will help you optimize your portfolio for maximum effectiveness.

### Test Across All Devices and Browsers

You must also confirm that your portfolio works consistently across a variety of devices, screen resolutions, and web browsers.

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid

- Too Many Effects: Having too many animations, colors or effects will hurt performance and distract \[visitors\] from what is most important: your work.

- Too Much Work: You want to focus on quality over quantity. Don't try to showcase every single piece of work you've ever created; instead, pick out your 3-6 best pieces and provide an overview of why they stand out.

- Neglecting Mobile Use: A lot of recruiters view portfolios via mobile devices; therefore, if a recruiter views your portfolio via mobile and has a negative experience, that creates a negative impression.

- Not Keeping Up with the Times: Be sure to constantly update your portfolio with any new work you have completed, any updated skills you have acquired, and accurate contact information.

- No Live Demos: \[if possible, it\] is important to have a live demo/working version of each piece of work in addition to screenshots/descriptions.


## Final Thoughts

A great developer portfolio template can make it easier to showcase your technical skills, projects and the entire professional path you've taken while searching for work in today's competitive tech job market. By selecting the appropriate template, customizing it to fit your unique needs and adding high-quality projects with valuable content that accurately reflects your abilities, your portfolio becomes a valuable resource to help open doors to new and exciting job opportunities.

The best Developer portfolios provide the ideal balance between visual appeal, high-quality technical demonstrations, and polished professional presentation versus personal authenticity; that is, they must tell a complete story with minimal distractions about your technical expertise and development experience.

If you are just beginning to explore your options as a developer, or you are an established developer in search of new opportunities, taking the time to build a high-quality developer portfolio will pay dividends in terms of increased exposure, greater opportunities for interviews/hire, and greater chances of being promoted or transitioned into a more advanced role.

Your developer portfolio should be viewed as a constantly evolving document; therefore, you should continually add new work to your portfolio, refine the way you present yourself and your skills, as well as ensure that your skill sets are kept current. Your developer portfolio should not only show what you've done; it should also represent who you will become as a developer.

## [Your UX portfolio is your sales pitch](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7809a993de06ecdbdc48c "Your UX portfolio is your sales pitch") Your UX portfolio is your sales pitch

![Your UX portfolio is your sales pitch](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3Ae211be7c-7bf6-4c9c-ad0f-a86ace6846c0%3Ayour_ux_portfolio_is_your_sales_pitch.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-8055-8a4c-e924996c764d&cache=v2)Your UX portfolio is your sales pitch

Too many designers treat their portfolio like a digital scrapbook, [crammed with every project](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/choose-the-right-projects-for-your-portfolio) they’ve ever touched, hoping something sticks.

> **Your portfolio isn’t about preserving your past. It’s about selling your future.**

[Hiring managers](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/hiring-manager-advice-ux-design-interviews) don’t want a history lesson. They want a reason to talk to you, fast.

If your current portfolio feels more “here’s everything I’ve done” and less “here’s why I’m the one you need,” don’t worry. You’re not alone.

This article will walk you through 6 no-fluff rules to turn your portfolio from a static archive into a high-converting asset.

## [6 rules to make your UX portfolio the biggest asset:](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7800585ebdc3c82b52437 "6 rules to make your UX portfolio the biggest asset:") 6 rules to make your UX portfolio the biggest asset:

### [1. Think strategy, not scrapbook](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780869f31fbc9a4b7f5c8 "1. Think strategy, not scrapbook") 1\. Think strategy, not scrapbook

![Think strategy, not scrapbook](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3Ae7442fd0-d1a8-4101-b029-019e52da8c4f%3Athink_strategy_not_scrapbook.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-80c2-b99e-e29ee01bdef9&cache=v2)Think strategy, not scrapbook

**The problem:** Most portfolios look like someone emptied their entire design folder onto a website and called it a day.

Look, I get it. You're proud of that logo you designed for your cousin's food truck. And sure, that website you built for your mom's book club shows your skills.

But [hiring managers](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/5-tips-to-nail-ux-design-interviews) don't care about your journey. They care about whether you can solve their problems. Your portfolio needs strategy, not sentiment.

#### [🔻 Focus on your positioning](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7808fb9d9c4962b28f863 "🔻 Focus on your positioning") 🔻 Focus on your positioning

Before you add a single project, ask yourself: _"What type of designer do I want to be known as?"_

Are you the fintech UX specialist? The B2B product design guru? The mobile-first interaction designer? Pick a lane and own it.

#### [🔻 Showcase relevant projects](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780d38407d64d6407f01d "🔻 Showcase relevant projects") 🔻 Showcase relevant projects

This is where most people mess up. They think more is better. Wrong.

Quality beats quantity every single time. I'd rather see three killer projects that perfectly match the role than twelve mediocre ones that confuse your narrative.

### [2. Explain your rationale](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780059667c8a5435c2a0c "2. Explain your rationale") 2\. Explain your rationale

![Explain your rationale](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3Ae39c361a-16b9-4676-a715-a45f93982043%3Aexplain_your_rationale.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-8055-a097-c59fd540e9a2&cache=v2)Explain your rationale

**The problem:** Most portfolios are like magic tricks, lots of flashy results with zero explanation of how you got there.

Hiring managers aren't just buying your final designs. They're buying your brain. They want to see how you think, how you solve problems, and how you make decisions under pressure.

#### [🔻 Provide evidence of research & iteration](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb78009b68eed412bc75bf8 "🔻 Provide evidence of research & iteration") 🔻 Provide evidence of research & iteration

Don't just show the polished final product. Show the messy middle.

Include your research artifacts. Show your [wireframe](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/how-to-ux-wireframe) iterations. Document your [design evolution](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/how-designers-approach-the-design-process-from-start-to-finish). This isn't about being thorough—it's about proving you didn't just guess your way to a solution.

#### [🔻 Be clear on how you got to the solution](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780c6841ee11dc7d54bf6 "🔻 Be clear on how you got to the solution") 🔻 Be clear on how you got to the solution

Walk me through your thinking. What constraints did you face? What trade-offs did you make? What would you do differently next time?

This [storytelling](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/guide-to-ux-storytelling) separates senior designers from juniors. Juniors show solutions. Seniors show systems of thinking.

#### [🔻 Highlight your decisions & tradeoffs](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7808e8d21d6f5f2e88a35 "🔻 Highlight your decisions & tradeoffs") 🔻 Highlight your decisions & tradeoffs

Every design decision is a trade-off. Show that you understand this.

Maybe you [prioritized accessibility](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/7-principles-for-inclusive-accesible-ux-designs) over visual flourish. Perhaps you chose faster loading times over rich animations. Document these choices. It shows [strategic thinking](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/9-essential-skills-for-ux-career-growth#5.-strategic-thinking).

💡

**Pro tip:** Use this framework for each project:

- **The challenge:** _What problem were you solving?_

- **The constraints:** _What limitations did you face?_

- **The approach:** _How did you tackle it?_

- **The trade-offs:** _What did you sacrifice and why?_

- **The result:** _What was the outcome?_

**Remember:** Good design is 80% reasoning, 20% aesthetics.

### [3. Highlight your impact](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780fca562d575e8be928a "3. Highlight your impact") 3\. Highlight your impact

![Highlight your impact](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3A2b6da588-c343-4914-9dfa-e1b260249bc5%3Ahighlight_your_impact.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-80b3-b11d-f14e782dfdc5&cache=v2)Highlight your impact

**The problem:** Designers love talking about process but hate talking about outcomes. This is business suicide.

Your [beautiful mockups](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/the-difference-between-wireframes-mockups-and-prototypes#what-are-mockups) mean nothing if they didn't move the needle. Hiring managers want to know: _**Did your work actually matter?**_

#### [🔻 Start each project with the results](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780b0ab14fe302a059257 "🔻 Start each project with the results") 🔻 Start each project with the results

Flip the script. Lead with impact, then explain how you got there.

❌ Instead of: "I redesigned the checkout flow..."

✅ Try: "Increased conversion rates by 23% through checkout flow optimization..."

See the difference? One focuses on what you did. The other focuses on what you achieved.

#### [🔻 No metrics? Use client or user feedback](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780f782eed0f8bee57d38 "🔻 No metrics? Use client or user feedback") 🔻 No metrics? Use client or user feedback

Not every project has clean analytics. That's okay. Use qualitative feedback instead.

[Customer testimonials](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/ux-designer-client-testimonials-guide), user quotes, stakeholder praise—these all count as impact. The key is proving your work mattered to real people.

### [4. Remove the noise](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780079baef3c7d1fef94c "4. Remove the noise") 4\. Remove the noise

![Remove the noise](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3A2511b233-936a-4051-98e2-939b5d16f24a%3ARemove_the_noise.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-8045-bd97-f898acef4fd3&cache=v2)Remove the noise

**The problem:** Most portfolios suffer from digital hoarding.

Too much text. Too many projects. Too many bells and whistles. The result? Cognitive overload for anyone trying to evaluate your work.

#### [🔻 Ruthlessly edit](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780f88509e271c65e26c7 "🔻 Ruthlessly edit") 🔻 **Ruthlessly edit**

Your portfolio should be like a good espresso—concentrated and potent.

Cut unnecessary words. Remove redundant projects. Eliminate anything that doesn't serve your narrative.

Remember: You're not documenting your entire career. You're building a highlight reel.

#### [🔻 Avoid overwhelming walls of text](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780d980a6d46a01e9ede5 "🔻 Avoid overwhelming walls of text") 🔻 Avoid overwhelming walls of text

Hiring managers skim, they don't read. Break up text with:

- White space

- Bullet points

- Subheadings

- Visual breaks

- Short paragraphs (like this one)

#### [🔻 Structure page so it’s easy to skim](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780afa5f4e68cf77db818 "🔻 Structure page so it’s easy to skim") 🔻 Structure page so it’s easy to skim

[Hiring managers don’t read portfolios](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/who-looks-at-your-design-portfolio-during-hiring-process). They scan them. You’ve got 30 seconds (if you’re lucky) to hook them before they bounce.

Make your portfolio effortless to skim:

- Lead with results, not process

- Bold key takeaways so they pop

- Keep paragraphs snack-sized—2-3 lines max

- Use clear subheadings like: Problem → Solution → Outcome

Think of it like UX for your own work: if it’s hard to parse, it won’t get read.

💡

**Pro tip:** [Design your portfolio](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/11-common-ux-portfolio-mistakes-and-solutions) like a landing page. Use the “3-second test”. Can someone glance at any section of your page and answer:

- _What was the problem?_

- _What did you do?_

- _What changed?_

If not, tighten it up. Your portfolio isn’t a journal. It’s a sales tool. Treat every scroll as a pitch for your next job.

* * *

### [5. Build a digital product](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7806ba295de4325d37f0f "5. Build a digital product") 5\. Build a digital product

![Build a digital product](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3A727de136-6112-41a2-9655-b5964885330f%3Abuild_a_digital_product.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-80e3-90b4-d211cc48ab94&cache=v2)Build a digital product

**The problem:** Most people treat their portfolio like a college thesis, something you finish once and forget about. Wrong mindset.

Your portfolio is a living, breathing product. It needs regular updates, iterations, and improvements.

#### [🔻 Document ongoing design work](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780c1868ff521ff6de377 "🔻 Document ongoing design work") 🔻 Document ongoing design work

Don’t wait for the “perfect” [case study](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/how-to-write-ux-case-study). Start a simple habit: document while you design.

Screenshot flows. Capture feedback. Note your decisions. These breadcrumbs become portfolio gold later.

Build a draft [case study](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/struggle-to-highlight-impact-in-the-case-study-how-to-fix-it) folder in [Notion](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/best-ux-portfolio-website-builders-2025#notion) or [Figma](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/figma-tips-for-ux-designers), and drop assets in weekly. That way, you’re never starting from scratch.

#### [🔻 Update portfolio every 3-6 months](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780c191e9f277c7787295 "🔻 Update portfolio every 3-6 months") 🔻 Update portfolio every 3-6 months

Put it on your calendar, just like a performance review. Use this time to:

- Retire outdated work

- Add your latest projects

- Refine messaging to match your current strengths and goals

Your future opportunities depend on how well your current story is told.

#### [🔻 Drop old work that no longer represents you](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7802ab66cd81e122a1744 "🔻 Drop old work that no longer represents you") 🔻 Drop old work that no longer represents you

This is the hardest part for most designers. We get attached to our work.

But that [mobile app](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/5-ux-strategies-for-accessible-mobile-apps) you designed three years ago, probably doesn't represent your current skill level. And that's okay. Growth means leaving old work behind.

💡

**Pro tip:** Treat your portfolio like your product. Ask yourself quarterly:

- _Would I hire myself based on this?_

- _Does this reflect where I want to go next?_

- _What’s the weakest link, and can I replace it?_

The best designers aren’t just talented, they’re intentional about how they show up. Your portfolio is your proof of that.

* * *

### [6. Paint a picture](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7806db425ee8a11a8ff86 "6. Paint a picture") 6\. Paint a picture

![Paint a picture](https://www.notion.so/image/attachment%3A9cd0700a-55fe-46dc-9d21-208c1c0d336a%3APaint_a_picture.png?table=block&id=25c2a971-edb7-8079-8ea8-f0c0c2f08002&cache=v2)Paint a picture

**The problem:** Too many portfolios feel like robot resumes… clean, correct, and completely forgettable.

They show what you did, but not why it mattered to you. Or who you are behind the pixels.

But hiring isn’t just about skills. It’s about trust, chemistry, and culture fit. [People don’t hire portfolios](https://uxplaybook.org/faq/stand-out-as-a-junior-designer). They hire people.

#### [🔻 Connect your skills, experiences, and future goals](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7804a9a01c2b738aa3a1f "🔻 Connect your skills, experiences, and future goals") 🔻 Connect your skills, experiences, and future goals

Your portfolio shouldn’t just say “I did this.” It should say “Here’s why I care and where I’m headed.”

Weave a thread between:

- **Your past:** _What drew you into design?_

- **Your present:** _What types of problems energize you?_

- **Your future:** _Where do you want to grow next?_

This signals self-awareness and ambition. Both matter more than pixel perfection.

#### [🔻 Show the impact of the problems you’re solving](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb7807082b7d2b424e5d3fe "🔻 Show the impact of the problems you’re solving") 🔻 Show the impact of the problems you’re solving

❌ **Instead of:** “Redesigned onboarding for mobile.”

✅ **Say:** “Helped new users feel confident in the first 60 seconds—retention improved by 18%.”

Frame your work through the lens of human value:

- _Who did this help?_

- _What changed for them?_

- _Why does it matter?_

This is how you move from “nice visuals” to “must-hire mindset.”

#### [🔻 Tell them what you want next](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780a49657d4f906f98dc4 "🔻 Tell them what you want next") 🔻 Tell them what you want next

Let people know what you’re looking for next. It doesn’t make you rigid. It makes you directional:

- _Want to mentor junior designers?_

- _Interested in ethical AI or civic tech?_

- _Thrive in early-stage chaos or crave mature systems?_

Clarity gives companies a reason to choose you, because your goals align with theirs.

💡

**Pro tip:** Write a Personal Manifesto. Instead of a boring “About Me,” write 3 short sections:

- **What I value**(e.g. Clarity, empathy, momentum)

- **How I work** (e.g. I ask the dumb questions. I move fast, then refine.)

- **What’s next** (e.g. I'm looking for a role where I can mentor, own strategy, and build products that matter.)

This isn’t fluff, it’s signal. And it’s often what hiring managers remember most.

* * *

## [UX Portfolio: 5 Do’s and 5 Don’ts](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780ceb53de99d58a948fc "UX Portfolio: 5 Do’s and 5 Don’ts") **UX Portfolio: 5 Do’s and 5 Don’ts**

❌

#### [What your UX portfolio is NOT](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb78007997edaa4a0b68ccf "What your UX portfolio is NOT") **What your UX portfolio is NOT**

- **A project graveyard:** Dumping every design you've ever done shows effort, but not judgment. Curate with intention.

- **A personal scrapbook:** It’s not about what you love. It’s about what your audience needs to see to trust and hire you.

- **A step-by-step diary:** Yes, process matters—but if it reads like a thesis, you’ve lost them. Make it sharp, visual, and skimmable.

- **A static archive:** Your portfolio should evolve with your skills, interests, and positioning. If it's 2 years old, it's out of date.

- **A solo performance:** [UX is collaborative](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/collaboration-with-working-styles-ux-designers). Show how you worked with others—PMs, engineers, users. Teamwork matters.

✅

#### [What your UX portfolio IS](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/6-ux-portfolio-rules-get-hired-2026\#25c2a971edb780e1a47ce292c24c315c "What your UX portfolio IS") **What your UX portfolio IS**

- **A curated narrative:** It’s a story about your design journey—where you’ve been, what you care about, and where you're headed.

- **A trust-building tool:** Hiring is high-risk. Your portfolio reduces doubt by proving you solve real problems, not just make pretty screens.

- **A strategic filter:** Showcase the kind of work you want more of. Your portfolio attracts the roles you’re best aligned for.

- **A demonstration of thinking:** Anyone can mock up [UI](https://uxplaybook.org/articles/how-to-improve-your-ui-design-skills). You show your value by revealing how you think, make decisions, and solve messy problems.

- **A conversation starter:** Your portfolio isn’t the end of the process—it’s the beginning. Design it to spark interest and lead to deeper discussions.

Thousands of design portfolios exist on the internet, each with a talented designer behind it looking to attract clients. To stand out, your portfolio must be unique, compelling, and skills-driven.
